title: Beef, steak, ribeye, lean only eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Ribeye steak is a cut from the beef rib section, known for its tenderness and rich beefy flavor. This version uses only the lean portion without visible fat, making it more diet‑friendly while retaining the characteristic taste and texture of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name ribeye comes from the eye‑shaped muscle in the rib area that gives the cut its distinctive marbling.
Lean ribeye is often favored in Asian cuisines where a clean meat flavor is prized.
Beef is a rich source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Traditionally, ribeye is grilled or pan‑seared to medium doneness to keep it juicy.
In the United States, ribeye ranks among the most popular steaks in steakhouses.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Lean ribeye provides about 22 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Heme iron in beef helps improve blood formation and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Lean steak contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Even lean cuts contain some saturated fat, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria such as E. coli or salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef proteins.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Beef is rich in purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ribeye is best cooked over high heat—grill, cast‑iron skillet, or broiler. Aim for medium doneness to keep it juicy. Let the steak sit at room temperature for 20‑30 minutes before cooking and rest for 5‑10 minutes after cooking so the juices redistribute. Serve with vegetables, salads, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, and use within 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag, where it retains quality for 6‑12 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.
